lesson.title: Request for Comments: How the Internet Writes Its Own Rulebook
lesson.summary: An RFC is a permanently numbered document, published through the process the IETF now runs, that defines an internet protocol or records a technical decision, turning a protocol design into a citable standard.
lesson.body:
The internet's protocols are documented in a series called RFCs, which stands for Request for Comments, and the name is a genuine piece of history rather than a marketing choice. In April 1969, Steve Crocker wrote the very first one, RFC 1, describing early ARPANET host software, and he deliberately chose a modest, informal title rather than something like "Official Specification," because the goal was to invite discussion among a small community of researchers rather than hand down an edict. More than five decades and thousands of documents later, the internet's core protocols, including the ones behind email, the web, and routing itself, are still published under that same unassuming name.

Not every RFC carries the same weight, and the category system is worth knowing. Standards Track documents, which start as Proposed Standards and can be elevated to full Internet Standards, define protocols the community expects widespread implementations to follow, and fully adopted ones are additionally given a separate STD number. Informational and Experimental RFCs describe things worth recording without asking anyone to implement them, Best Current Practice documents capture operational guidance, and a handful, published every April Fools' Day, are deliberate jokes, such as RFC 2549, which describes transmitting internet traffic by pigeon. Once an RFC is published, its number and text never change again. If a protocol needs correcting or updating, the fix appears as a brand new RFC that formally obsoletes the old one.

TCP itself is a clean example of how this works. RFC 793, published in 1981, defined TCP and served as its authoritative reference for over four decades. In 2022, RFC 9293 was published, consolidating decades of accumulated clarifications and errata into a single updated document, and it formally obsoletes RFC 793. Both documents remain permanently readable and citable, since nothing is ever deleted from the RFC series, but only RFC 9293 is the current standard an implementer should follow today. This is exactly the kind of stability and traceability a protocol needs once millions of independently built devices depend on it.

An RFC is where the protocol and standard ideas from the previous two chapters actually meet. A protocol's syntax, semantics, and timing rules have to be written down somewhere precise enough for two unrelated engineering teams to implement it identically, and the RFC series is the document format the internet community settled on for doing exactly that. The main body that manages this process today is the IETF, which the next chapter covers in detail, but the RFC series itself predates the IETF's formal founding and has simply carried forward as the accepted publication venue.

One more feature of RFCs is easy to overlook but genuinely important: every one of them is free to read, with no membership fee, paywall, or licensing agreement standing between a curious student and the exact document that defines how HTTP or IP actually works. That openness was not an accident. It reflects a deliberate choice by the early internet community to let anyone verify, implement, and build on these rules, and it is a large part of why the internet grew as quickly and as openly as it did.
